title: Solubility & solubility curves
examples: Teacher, what does it mean when a solution is saturated?
How do I use a solubility curve to predict how much salt I can dissolve?
Can you show me an example of crystallisation in the lab?

explain.say: Today we are learning about solubility in solutions. Solubility means how much substance can dissolve in a liquid.
A saturated solution holds the maximum amount of solute possible. It cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature.
Solubility curves help us see how solubility changes with temperature. They show the maximum amount that can dissolve.
Crystallisation is the process of forming solid crystals from a solution. This often happens when the temperature drops.
For example, when we cool a saturated salt solution, some of the excess solute will come out as crystals.
In real life, making rock salt crystals uses this idea. They cool a concentrated brine solution to grow large crystals.

faq.q: What is the difference between a saturated and an unsaturated solution?
faq.a: A saturated solution holds the maximum amount of dissolved substance possible at that temperature. An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more solute.
asks: Can I add more stuff to an unsaturated solution?

faq.q: Why does cooling a solution cause crystals to form?
faq.a: Cooling lowers the solubility limit, meaning the solution can no longer hold all the dissolved solute. The excess solid precipitates out.
asks: Does temperature really affect how much dissolves?
Is it always the temperature that causes this?

faq.q: What do the points on a solubility curve represent?
faq.a: Each point shows the maximum mass of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specific temperature. The line connects these limits.
asks: How do I read the curve if the units are different?
Does the curve change if I change the solvent?

faq.q: Is crystallisation the same as precipitating?
faq.a: Crystallisation is a specific type of precipitation where the solid forms in a highly ordered, crystal structure. Precipitation is the general term for any solid forming.
asks: Are these terms interchangeable in chemistry?
What makes a crystal structure special?

faq.q: If I dissolve sugar in hot water, is the solution saturated?
faq.a: Not necessarily. If you can still dissolve a little more sugar, it is unsaturated. You need to add until no more dissolves.
asks: How do I test if a solution is saturated?
Does the initial temperature matter for saturation?

facts: Solubility is the maximum concentration of a solute in a solvent.
Most solid solutes become less soluble as the temperature decreases.
Crystallisation occurs when a solution becomes supersaturated or cools below saturation point.
Solubility curves graph solubility against temperature.

quiz.say: If a solubility curve shows solubility increasing as temperature rises, what happens when you cool the solution?
quiz.why: Because the solution can hold less solute at lower temperatures, the excess solid falls out.

wrong.0: This is tempting because solutions are usually dissolved, but the limit is broken upon cooling.
wrong.1: Cooling always pushes the solution towards or past its saturation point.
wrong.2: The process of cooling only changes the temperature, not the liquid itself.

quiz.say: A solution that holds the maximum amount of solute possible is called:
quiz.why: Saturated is the specific chemical term for a solution at its limit of dissolving capacity.

wrong.0: Concentrated is a general term; saturated is the specific state at the limit.
wrong.1: Unsaturated means it can still dissolve more solute.
wrong.3: Supersaturated means it holds more than the maximum, which is unstable.

quiz.say: When making crystals, what is the best way to ensure the crystals are pure?
quiz.why: Slow cooling allows the solute molecules time to arrange themselves into a perfect, ordered crystal lattice.

wrong.0: Heating increases solubility, but it does not control the rate of crystal formation.
wrong.2: Boiling too fast can trap impurities within the forming crystals.
wrong.3: A filter removes solid material, but it does not control the crystal structure.
